comparison: Both evaluate the pupillary block mechanism (C6, C7, C31, C33-C35). OpenEval finds the mechanism well-supported by converging experimental evidence from multiple modalities. Peer reviewers fundamentally challenge this, with Reviewer 3 stating the mechanism is 'almost surely not what is illustrated' and arguing for direct TM blockade by oil instead. Editors request manometric proof of the proposed mechanism.

Both address IOP measurements and size-dependent effects (C8-C10, C36-C37). OpenEval finds reproducible IOP elevation with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers identify 'a huge error' regarding timing of measurements under anesthesia and note a logical contradiction: if dilation allows aqueous to reach meshwork, IOP should decrease not increase. Editors request reconciliation of this inconsistency.

Both evaluate IOP data consistency (C11-C12). OpenEval finds clear size-dependent effects with appropriate statistical analysis. Peer reviewers challenge statistical rigor, noting 'primary data are not only not convincing, the data are not even statistically tested' and questioning whether error bars show major variability rather than consistent elevation. Sample size and measurement frequency are questioned.

Both address functional progression over time (C13-C14). OpenEval finds well-documented progression from 1wpi to 8wpi with statistical significance. Peer reviewers state 'the manner in which the data is presented...do not show that there is progression over time' and request clearer presentation. The secondary analysis comparing to week 1 rather than baseline is problematic.

Both evaluate early functional deficits (C15-C16). OpenEval acknowledges potential optical confounding from SO that cannot be fully resolved. Peer reviewers question whether 'OKR and PERG are reliable functional assessments if visual acuity is impaired due to difference in refractive index of SO' and suggest lack of progression indicates SO itself causes decreased amplitudes.

Both address PERG measurements (C17). OpenEval notes progression is well-documented but acknowledges optical confounding from SO. Peer reviewers question reliability given potential optical interference and lack of proper baseline controls, requesting acknowledgment that 'PERG amplitude reduction may be due to the presence of the SO itself.' Lack of progression compared to week 1 is noted as problematic.

Both evaluate RGC loss quantification (C18-C19). OpenEval finds quantitative histological data showing time-dependent neurodegeneration with appropriate statistics. Peer reviewers identify major inconsistency between Figure 3 (12% survival) and Figure 4 (60% survival) at 8 weeks. Reviewer 3 notes 'such massive RGC death is only seen in severe crush or transection injury' and requests demonstration this is not ischemia-reperfusion.

Both address rate and severity of RGC loss (C20). OpenEval finds temporal pattern supports interpretation though confounded by optical effects. Peer reviewers state 'the rate of RGC loss in this model is excessive' and 'represents a very severe damage, similar to the situation of complete transection' that 'does not replicate the most cases of glaucoma.' Request for histology showing axonal transport block to prove glaucoma-like mechanism.

Both evaluate correlation to human glaucoma and RGC resilience (C44-C46). OpenEval finds correlation reasonable though somewhat speculative, with RGC resilience interpretation supported by temporal patterns. Peer reviewers state damage 'does not replicate the most cases of glaucoma' due to excessive severity, question whether model represents secondary vs. primary glaucoma, and request demonstration this is not 'more an ischemia-reperfusion experiment.'

Both evaluate control experiments ruling out SO toxicity (C21-C23). OpenEval finds these critical controls effectively demonstrate neurodegeneration is IOP-dependent. Peer reviewers accept these control experiments as valid, with Reviewer 1 acknowledging the model 'differs from other established models' in having 'minimal tissue damage and inflammation.' This is a rare area of agreement.

Both address reversibility after SO removal (C24-C25). OpenEval finds rapid IOP normalization demonstrates reversibility and supports preserved TM function. Peer reviewers acknowledge reversibility as a potential advantage, with Reviewer 3 noting it is 'potentially useful adjunct' for studying various periods of IOP elevation. No direct challenge to reversibility data itself.

Both evaluate mechanism interpretation and practical aspects (C38, C74). OpenEval finds evidence supports the proposed mechanism though acknowledges TM occlusion cannot be completely excluded. Peer reviewers question the interpretation, stating mechanism is 'almost surely not what is illustrated' and suggesting direct TM blockade. Also note 'waiting 15 minutes is not only completely impractical' and question the artificial anesthetic state.

Both characterize model features and limitations (C50-C51, C55, C58). OpenEval finds characterization reasonable with appropriate acknowledgment of limitations regarding chronic primary glaucoma. Peer reviewers note this type of secondary glaucoma 'is rare since surgeons prophylactically create peripheral iridotomies,' question whether model replicates most glaucoma cases given excessive damage, and state severe damage 'may make it harder for any protectant to block cell death.'

Both address compartmentalization and mechanism (C71, C78). OpenEval finds speculation reasonable though unresolved. Peer reviewers directly challenge this, with Reviewer 3 stating it is 'silly to assume that the iris is going to bow forward with an anterior chamber full of oil' and Reviewer 2 noting TanoLab 'is incapable of assessing the actual IOP value in the posterior part of the eye.' Editors request manometric readings to prove compartmentalization.

Both evaluate claimed advantages (C72-C73). OpenEval finds advantages supported by experimental results including low variability. Peer reviewers question these claims, noting 'every model in mice shows corneal enlargement...in the range reported here, so further studies of clarity need to be presented' and questioning whether visual function assessments are reliable given SO's refractive index. Severe damage may limit utility for neuroprotectant screening.

Both address limitations of existing models (C59-C61). OpenEval finds these claims accurately summarize published literature. Peer reviewers directly refute the success rate claim, stating 'Published data show that 95% of microbead injected mouse eyes achieve significant IOP elevation...This is not a "low success rate" and is actually better than the 80% rate reported here.' Also notes variability in RGC loss is typical for human OAG.

Both evaluate background claims on glaucoma definition and pathophysiology (C3-C5). OpenEval finds these supported by appropriate citations. Peer reviewers provide detailed corrections: definition is 'incorrect and inexact' and should specify 'injury to the axons of RGC at the optic nerve head'; 'the risk factor is the level of the IOP, not elevated IOP' since half or more with OAG do not have elevated IOP; therapy aims to lower IOP sufficiently from baseline, not 'normalize' it.

OpenEval evaluates clinical background on SO-induced secondary glaucoma in humans (C26-C30) as supported by appropriate citations and standard clinical understanding. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific background claims.

OpenEval evaluates general glaucoma background (C1-C2, C70) as supported by appropriate citations. Peer reviewers address related claims (C3-C5) in R16 but do not specifically evaluate C1, C2, or C70.

OpenEval identifies speculative interpretations and acknowledged limitations (C47-C49, C54, C71, C76, C79) as uncertain, noting important confounds that limit interpretation. While peer reviewers question various aspects of the model throughout their reviews, no single peer result specifically groups these limitation and speculation claims together.

OpenEval evaluates citations on vascular changes in human glaucoma (C52-C53) as supported literature providing context for ischemic mechanisms. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these vascular literature claims.

OpenEval evaluates rationale for model development (C56, C67-C69) as supported by established knowledge and reasonable inference. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these rationale claims, though peer reviewers question the model's utility throughout.

OpenEval evaluates methodological citations (C77, C80) as appropriate references supporting experimental approach. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these methodological reference claims.

OpenEval evaluates detailed experimental methods (C81-C102) as internally consistent and technically sound, though notes some details about blinding and randomization could be more explicit. No corresponding peer review evaluation found systematically addressing the methods section claims, though reviewers question specific methodological aspects throughout.
